title: Dynamics and Control Laboratory
text:
The Dynamics and Control Laboratory at The Cooper Union connects mathematical modeling, feedback control, and physical experimentation. Its experimental platforms enable the development and validation of control methods, the investigation of coordinated motion, and the physical visualization of dynamical systems.



Indoor flight arena and control workstations at The Cooper Union.




The laboratory operates an indoor quadrotor flight arena with a six-camera Vicon motion capture system, Lighthouse positioning infrastructure, and Crazyflie nano quadrotors. Real-time motion measurements and feedback controllers support autonomous flight, trajectory tracking, and coordinated multivehicle experiments.



The following projects illustrate laboratory research and faculty-advised student engineering activities.




The motion-capture-based flight platform has been used to demonstrate hovering, trajectory tracking, and coordinated motion of multiple quadrotors. Experiments connect mathematical models and simulations with measured flight behavior, including circular trajectories and synchronized formations.
As part of his master’s thesis work in 2019, Justin Rooney developed an interactive magic wand demonstration in which the wand’s motion determines the hover set-point for a swarm of Crazyflie nano quadrotors. The vehicles respond collectively, producing coordinated motion reminiscent of migratory bird formations.
Watch the drone tornado formation
Watch the magic wand demonstration
Related work: Justin Rooney, master’s thesis abstract (2020).





Quadrotor vehicles used in the laboratory.









Quadrotors serve as physical representations of dynamical systems governed by differential equations. Developed initially by Joon Kim and Jaehyeon Park through the Vertically Integrated Projects (VIP) course, the hand-tracking interface uses computer vision and MediaPipe to control quadrotors. During summer research in 2024, Joon Kim extended the work with interactive demonstrations of mass–spring–damper systems, coupled oscillators, and pendulum motion. After release, a vehicle follows the motion prescribed by the mathematical model.
Watch the hand-tracking demonstration
Initial hand-tracking project: Joon Kim and Jaehyeon Park, VIP38XA — The Autonomy of “Smart” Cities. Summer 2024 research extensions and video demonstration: Joon Kim.





Poster: Hand Tracking Drone Control Using MediaPipe.









A gyroscopically actuated vehicle project investigates three-dimensional rigid-body dynamics and the generation of control moments using rotating flywheels. The work combines reference-frame-based modeling, angular momentum analysis, numerical simulation, mechanical design, and prototype development.
The project illustrates how geometric descriptions of motion inform the design and analysis of unconventional vehicles.
Related publication: J. Chen et al., “Part 1: Gyroscopic Control of Robotic Smart Vehicles Using SO(3)”, Proceedings of the ASME 2023 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition, IMECE2023-113518 (2024).





CAD rendering of a gyroscopically actuated vehicle.









In 2024, I served as faculty advisor to The Cooper Union student team participating in the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA) Design/Build/Fly competition in Wichita, Kansas.
The team designed, manufactured, and flight-tested a radio-controlled aircraft for an urban air mobility mission. The competition called for delivery, medical transport, and urban taxi configurations, requiring the team to integrate aerodynamic design, structural analysis, fabrication, and flight testing.
The aircraft successfully flew at the competition, although stable landing remained a challenge. The project provided students with experience in iterative engineering development and testing under real-world constraints.

title: A Projection-Based Derivation of the Equations of Motion for the Moving Frame Method for Multi-Body Dynamics
text:
PDF



CitationBibTeX citation:@misc{m._luchtenburg,_mili_shah,_thomas_j._impelluso,_thorstein_ravneberg_rykkje2022,
  author = {M. Luchtenburg, Mili Shah, Thomas J. Impelluso, Thorstein
    Ravneberg Rykkje, Dirk},
  title = {A {Projection-Based} {Derivation} of the {Equations} of
    {Motion} for the {Moving} {Frame} {Method} for {Multi-Body}
    {Dynamics}},
  date = {2022-01-25},
  url = {https://realdirk.github.io/publications/luchtenburg2021asme/},
  doi = {10.1115/IMECE2021-72324},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {The moving frame method for multi-body dynamics,
    established by Murakami in {[}10{]} and {[}11{]}, embodies a
    consistent notation and mathematical framework that simplifies the
    derivation of equations of motion of complex systems. The derivation
    of the equations of motion follows Hamilton’s principle and requires
    the calculation of virtual angular velocities and the corresponding
    virtual rotational displacements. The goal of this paper is to
    present a projection-based approach, which only requires knowledge
    of Euler’s first and second law, that results in the same equation
    of motion. The constraints need not satisfy d’Alembert’s principle
    and the projection is based on a generalization of Gauss’ principle
    of least constraint {[}14{]}. One advantage of the proposed method
    is that it avoids variational principles and therefore is more
    accessible to undergraduate students. In addition, the final form of
    the equation of motion is more easily understood. We motivate our
    approach using the example of the simple pendulum, derive the main
    result, and apply the methodology for derivation of the equations of
    motion for a modified Chaplygin sleigh and a rotary pendulum.}
}
For attribution, please cite this work as:
M. Luchtenburg, Mili Shah, Thomas J. Impelluso, Thorstein Ravneberg
Rykkje, Dirk. 2022. “A Projection-Based Derivation of the
Equations of Motion for the Moving Frame Method for Multi-Body
Dynamics.” In ASME IMECE 2021. Preprint, January 25. https://doi.org/10.1115/IMECE2021-72324.

title: Modelling the Motion of a 2-Arm ROV
text:

CitationBibTeX citation:@misc{r._saure,_sondre_h._iversen,_andreas_b._snekkevik,_rose_gebhardt,_zhiyang_chen,_christopher_mignano,_dirk_luchtenburg,_thomas_j._impelluso2020,
  author = {R. Saure, Sondre H. Iversen, Andreas B. Snekkevik, Rose
    Gebhardt, Zhiyang Chen, Christopher Mignano, Dirk Luchtenburg,
    Thomas J. Impelluso, Marius},
  title = {Modelling the {Motion} of a {2-Arm} {ROV}},
  date = {2020-01-21},
  url = {https://realdirk.github.io/publications/saure2019asme/},
  doi = {10.1115/IMECE2019-10282},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {Norway conducts operations on a variety of structures in
    the North Sea; e.g. oilrigs, monopole windmills, subsea trees. These
    structures often require subsea installation, observation, and
    maintenance. A remotely operated vehicle (ROV) can assist in these
    operations. Automation of intended motion is the desired goal. This
    paper researches the motion of an ROV induced by the motion of the
    robotic manipulators, motor torques, and added mass of fluid. This
    project builds upon a previous project that had one robotic arm;
    this time, there are two, but the method is unchanged. Furthermore,
    this work explores both the patterns in addressing such challenges,
    and an improved integration scheme. This research uses the Moving
    Frame Method (MFM) to carry out this project. In fact, this paper
    demonstrates the ease with which the MFM is extensible. Notable is
    that this work represents an international collaboration between an
    engineering school in Norway and one in the US. This work invites
    further research into improved numerical methods, solid/fluid
    interaction and the design of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUV).
    AUVs beckon an era of Artificial Intelligence when machines think,
    communicate and learn. Rapidly deployable software implementations
    will be essential to this task.}
}

  author = {Song; Dirk Luchtenburg, Yeeho},
  title = {Using Compliant Leg Design for Impact Attenuation of Airdrop
    Landings of Quadruped Robots},
  date = {2017-07-24},
  url = {https://realdirk.github.io/publications/song2017ieee/},
  doi = {10.1109/ICRA.2017.7989427},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {Most airdropped cargo use a combination of one or more
    parachutes and an impact attenuation system to land safely. The
    latter adds cost, weight and complexity. However, by using their
    legs for impact attenuation, airdropped quadruped robots may avoid
    the need for such a system. In this paper, various leg
    configurations for attenuating impact of airborne landings were
    studied and tested. Using simple lumped element models for
    simulation and analysis, a quadruped robot with a three-segment leg
    was designed and built. This model was validated with experiments
    with a small scale 20 cm-tall test robot. During the experiments,
    the test robot experienced 7.7 \$\textbackslash times\$ 10
    m/s\$\^{}2\$ or 7.9 g-acceleration when dropped from height of 37.85
    cm. This result is much better than the result of 1.4
    \$\textbackslash times\$ 10\$\^{}2\$ m/s\$\^{}2\$ or
    14.7g-acceleration when dropped at 10\% of the original height with
    the same robot equipped with rigid legs. Such compliant leg design
    could be potentially used for impact attenuation of airdrop landings
    of robots five times larger.}
}

title: Teaching
text:
My teaching and research inform one another. I bring ideas from dynamics, modeling, and control into the classroom, while the work of explaining fundamental concepts clearly often sharpens my own thinking. I view engineering education as an apprenticeship in engineering reasoning: students learn to formulate problems, choose and justify models, analyze their behavior, and assess what the results mean. Analytical work and computation support this process, but neither replaces physical understanding or engineering judgment.





An introduction to the mechanics of moving systems, organized around reference frames, geometric reasoning, and the systematic formulation of equations of motion. Analytical developments are supported by Python-based computation and simulation, with an emphasis on methods that extend naturally to three-dimensional problems in robotics, flight dynamics, and control.



An introduction to modeling, analysis, and design of feedback control systems. Students connect system dynamics to stability, transient and frequency response, and classical control design, using computation to test predictions and evaluate design choices.



A project-based course in which students address open-ended engineering problems. Emphasis is placed on defining a defensible problem, evaluating design alternatives, supporting decisions with analysis and evidence, and communicating results clearly.




Engineering Dynamics: A Geometric and Computational Companion (manuscript in development)
Developed alongside ME 200, this companion integrates geometric and frame-based mechanics with computational examples. Its purpose is to help students move from standard planar problems to the formulation and analysis of general three-dimensional motion.

title: Visualizing Physical Phenomena Using Swarming Nano Quadrotors
text:
The goal of this project is to use drones as analogies and metaphors of physical systems. For instance, a drone can mimic the motion of a mass-spring system. While the drone is hovering in mid-air the user pulls it down to provide an initial displacement, and the drone starts oscillating with a frequency determined by the physical parameters of the mass-spring system. Similarly, multiple drones can be used to visualize standing and moving waves.
Justin Rooney started this project as part of his M.Eng. thesis, PDF. 
This project is now continued as a VIP course. Students Aymane Saissi, Amelia Chan, and Jason Chen, implemented a swarming drones demo that visualizes a tornado motion.

title: Gyroscope Assisted Stair Climbing Car
text:
Inspired by the success of Seakeeper gyroscopic boat stabilization, this project has the ambitious goal of using gyroscopically generated torque to allow a car to climb up a set of stairs. The team is a group of five junior mechanical engineering students whose broad set of interests has allowed the scope of this project to include mathematical modeling and simulation, implementation of control schemes, sensor data acquisition, and mechanical design and manufacturing.
The initial design is a reaction wheel placed inside the frame of the car. The wheel is spun up to ridiculous speeds over the course of a few minutes, then a brake is suddenly applied. Conservation of momentum will cause the car to pitch upwards and bring the center of mass over one set of wheels. Subsequently the car can balance in that position through actuation of both the ground wheels and reaction wheel according to a control algorithm.

title: Ground robots
text: This research project seeks to employ ROS2, the iRobot Create3 robot, and the Vicon Motion Capture system available in the lab for either navigation or modeling of physical systems. The navigation aspect involves constructing a city-like environment within the Vicon system and enabling the Create3 robot to navigate through it, avoiding obstacles and reaching a specified destination. In the physical systems modeling aspect, the goal is to input mathematical equations representing systems and have the Create3 robot follow the corresponding paths. David Guo, Will Wu, Eric Xu, and David Yang are currently working as part of a VIP course to integrate various functions demonstrated in the video into a cohesive and operational system.

title: Research
text:
My research concerns the mathematical modeling, analysis, and control of dynamical systems. I am particularly interested in how mathematical representations reveal the structures governing system behavior and how these structures can be exploited for prediction and control.
Three closely connected themes run through my work.




Geometric structures, particularly invariant manifolds, provide insight into the behavior of nonlinear dynamical systems.
My current research investigates how invariant structures can be used to understand and control transport in nonlinear dynamical systems, with applications in astrodynamics. In collaboration with Prof. Shane D. Ross at Virginia Tech, this work includes hybrid control methods for transfers between invariant structures and the classification of chaotic trajectories in cislunar space.
Recent conference contributions include Hybrid MPC–OGY Control for Transport Between Invariant Structures with Application to Keplerian Maps (D. M. Luchtenburg and S. D. Ross) and Dynamical Classification of Chaotic Cislunar Trajectories via Resonance Structure (A. M. Lutz, D. M. Luchtenburg, A. Rawat, and S. D. Ross).





Invariant-manifold geometry in the standard map (\(K=0.9\)).









Complex dynamical systems often admit lower-dimensional representations that capture their essential behavior.
My contributions include reduced-order modeling of fluid flows, proper orthogonal decomposition, dynamic mode decomposition, and methods for long-time uncertainty propagation. Representative publications include On dynamic mode decomposition: Theory and applications and Long-time uncertainty propagation using generalized polynomial chaos and flow map composition.





Long-time uncertainty propagation in a double-gyre flow.









Mathematical modeling and dynamical systems theory provide the foundation for understanding and controlling physical systems.
My work combines theoretical and computational methods with experimental investigations, including ship stabilization, robotic systems, autonomous vehicles, and student-led research projects. An example is Seven Degrees-of-Freedom Model for the Roll Stabilization of Unstable Ships.

title: Seven Degrees-of-Freedom Model for the Roll Stabilization of Unstable Ships
text:
PDF 



CitationBibTeX citation:@article{shekhtman,_dirk_m._luchtenburg2019,
  author = {Shekhtman, Dirk M. Luchtenburg, David},
  title = {Seven {Degrees-of-Freedom} {Model} for the {Roll}
    {Stabilization} of {Unstable} {Ships}},
  journal = {ASME JDSMC 2019},
  date = {2019-03-25},
  url = {https://realdirk.github.io/publications/shekhtman2019asme/},
  doi = {10.1115/1.4042950},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {As demonstrated by the 2014 MV Sewol incident, the
    prevention of top heavy ship capsize is necessary to protect life
    and property aboard a ship. The goal of this paper is to prevent the
    capsize of ships, which lack a restoring torque about the roll axis,
    by using a feedback-controlled pendulum actuator. A seven
    degrees-of-freedom (7DOF) model is developed for a ship equipped
    with a pendulum actuator. The model is used to conduct parameter
    analyses on the pendulum length, pendulum mast height, pendulum
    mass, ship center of mass (COM) height, and the pendulum
    controller’s proportional feedback gain. The results of these
    analyses are depicted via time responses and phase plots. Key points
    for designing a pendulum actuator summarize simulation results,
    stating that the pendulum mass should be 3–7\% of the total ship
    mass, and the pendulum moment of inertia should be 0.5–1.0 times the
    roll moment of inertia of the ship.}
}

    Dirk Martin Luchtenburg, Zhekai},
  title = {A {Multisensor} {Data} {Fusion} {Approach} for {Simultaneous}
    {Localization} and {Mapping}},
  date = {2019-11-28},
  url = {https://realdirk.github.io/publications/jin2019ieee/},
  doi = {10.1109/ITSC.2019.8916930},
  langid = {en},
  abstract = {Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) has been an
    emerging research topic in the fields of robotics, autonomous
    driving, and unmanned aerial vehicles over the past thirty years.
    State of the art SLAM research is often inaccessible for
    undergraduate student researchers due to expensive hardware and
    difficult software setup. We present a cost-friendly vehicle
    research platform and a robust implementation of SLAM. Our SLAM
    algorithm fuses visual stereo image and 2D light detection and
    ranging (Lidar) data and uses loop closure for accurate odometry
    estimation. Our algorithm is benchmarked against other popular SLAM
    algorithms using the publicly available KITTI dataset and shown to
    be very accurate.}
}

title: About
text:
Dirk M. Luchtenburg is Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering at The Cooper Union. His research interests include nonlinear dynamics, mathematical modeling, and feedback control, with applications spanning fluid mechanics and autonomous systems.
He received his master’s degree in aerospace engineering from Delft University of Technology and his PhD in fluid mechanics from Technische Universität Berlin. Before joining The Cooper Union, he held research and teaching appointments at Princeton University.
His work brings together mathematical analysis, computational methods, and physical experimentation to understand and control dynamical systems. This perspective also informs his teaching, where mathematical foundations are connected to engineering applications.
For additional information, see his Curriculum vitae.
